{{Short description|Class of constitutive equations for viscoelastic fluids}}
The '''upper-convected Maxwell''' ('''UCM''') '''model''' is a generalisation of the [[Maxwell material]] for the case of large deformations using the [[upper-convected time derivative]]. The model was proposed by [[James G. Oldroyd]].  The concept is named after [[James Clerk Maxwell]]. It is the simplest observer independent [[constitutive equation]] for [[viscoelasticity]] and further is able to reproduce first normal stresses. Thus, it constitutes one of the most fundamental models for [[rheology]].

The model can be written as:
:<math> \mathbf{T} + \lambda \stackrel{\nabla}{\mathbf{T}} = 2\eta_0 \mathbf {D} </math>
where:
* <math>\mathbf{T}</math> is the [[Stress (physics)|stress]] [[tensor]];
* <math>\lambda</math> is the relaxation time;
* <math> \stackrel{\nabla}{\mathbf{T}} </math> is the [[upper-convected time derivative]] of stress tensor:
:<math> \stackrel{\nabla}{\mathbf{T}} = \frac{\partial}{\partial t} \mathbf{T} + \mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla \mathbf{T} - (\nabla \mathbf{v})^T \cdot \mathbf{T} - \mathbf{T} \cdot (\nabla \mathbf{v}) </math>
*<math>\mathbf{v}</math> is the fluid velocity and the gradient of a vector follows the convention <math> (\nabla{\mathbf{v}})_{ij} = \partial_i v_j</math>.
*<math>\eta_0</math> is material [[viscosity]] at steady [[simple shear]];
*<math>\mathbf {D}</math> is the [[Strain rate tensor|deformation rate tensor]].

The model can be derived either by applying the concept of observer invariance to the [[Maxwell material]] or by two different mesoscopic models, namely Hookean Dumbells<ref name="rogerswilliams">{{Cite book|last1=Öttinger |first1=H.C. | edition= 1st|title= Stochastic processes in polymeric fluids: tools and examples for developing simulation algorithms |publisher=[[Springer-Verlag]] | year=1996 | isbn=978-3-540-58353-0 |  doi= 10.1007/978-3-642-58290-5 }}</ref> or Temporary Networks.<ref>{{Cite book|title=The Structure and Rheology of Complex Fluids (Topics in Chemical Engineering): Larson, Ronald G.: 9780195121971: Amazon.com: Books|isbn=019512197X |last1=Larson |first1=Ronald G. |date=28 January 1999 |publisher=Oup USA }}</ref> Even though both microscopic model lead to the upper evolution equation for the stress, recent work pointed up the differences when accounting also for the stress fluctuations. <ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last1=Winters|first1=A.|last2=Öttinger|first2=H. C.|last3=Vermant|first3=J.|date=2024|title=Comparative analysis of fluctuations in viscoelastic stress: A comparison of the temporary network and dumbbell models|url=https://pubs.aip.org/aip/jcp/article/161/1/014901/3300367/Comparative-analysis-of-fluctuations-in|journal=Journal of Chemical Physics|language=en|volume=161 |pages=014901|doi=10.1063/5.0213660|arxiv=2404.19743}}</ref> 


==Case of the steady shear==
For this case only two components of the shear stress became non-zero:
:<math>T_{12}=\eta_0 \dot \gamma \, </math>
and
:<math>T_{11}=2 \eta_0 \lambda {\dot \gamma}^2 \, </math>
where <math>\dot \gamma</math> is the [[shear rate]].

Thus, the upper-convected Maxwell model predicts for the simple shear that [[shear stress]] to be proportional to the shear rate and the [[first difference of normal stresses]] (<math>T_{11}-T_{22}</math>) is proportional to the square of the shear rate, the [[second difference of normal stresses]] (<math>T_{22}-T_{33}</math>) is always zero. In other words, UCM predicts appearance of the first difference of normal stresses but does not predict [[Non-Newtonian fluid|non-Newtonian behavior]] of the shear viscosity nor the second difference of the normal stresses.

Usually quadratic behavior of the first difference of normal stresses and no second difference of the normal stresses is a realistic behavior of polymer melts at moderated shear rates, but constant viscosity is unrealistic and limits usability of the model.

==Case of start-up of steady shear==
For this case only two components of the shear stress became non-zero:
:<math>T_{12}=\eta_0 \dot \gamma \left(1-\exp\left(-\frac t \lambda\right)\right)</math>
and
:<math>T_{11}=2 \eta_0 \lambda {\dot \gamma}^2 \left(1 -\exp\left(-\frac t \lambda\right)\left(1+\frac t \lambda \right)\right)</math>

The equations above describe stresses gradually risen from zero the steady-state values.
The equation is only applicable, when the velocity profile in the [[shear flow]] is fully developed. Then the shear rate is constant over the channel height. If the start-up form a zero velocity distribution has to be calculated, the full set of PDEs has to be solved.

==Case of the steady state uniaxial extension or uniaxial compression==
For this case UCM predicts the normal stresses <math>\sigma=T_{11}-T_{22}=T_{11}-T_{33}</math> calculated by the following equation:
: <math>\sigma=\frac {2 \eta_0 \dot \epsilon} {1-2\lambda \dot \epsilon} + \frac {\eta_0 \dot \epsilon} {1+ \lambda \dot \epsilon}</math>
where <math>\dot \epsilon</math> is the elongation rate.

The equation predicts the elongation viscosity approaching <math>3 \eta_0</math> (the same as for the [[Newtonian fluid]]s) for the case of low elongation rate ( <math>\dot \epsilon \ll \frac 1 \lambda</math>) with fast deformation thickening with the steady state viscosity approaching infinity at some elongational rate (<math>\dot \epsilon_\infty = \frac 1 {2 \lambda}</math>) and at some compression rate (<math>\dot \epsilon_{-\infty} = -\frac 1 {\lambda}</math>). This behavior seems to be realistic.

==Case of small deformation==
For the case of small deformation the nonlinearities introduced by the upper-convected derivative disappear and the model becomes an ordinary model of [[Maxwell material]].
